utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom assisting us. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Both parties I think have indicated that they would like to address the Chamber. Prosecution first -- or is there any logical order in the matters you would like to raise? Or is there nothing?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't believe I -- good afternoon. I don't actually believe I indicated anything I wanted to address. I think Mr. Emmerson was going to address the witness for tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which might be --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But we would seek to call Mr. Dourel tomorrow and I think he would wish to address the Trial Chamber on why he doesn't wish Mr. Dourel to give evidence before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, is that the issue you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There were two issues. There's one relating to the next witness and the exhibits that the Prosecution has given notice of its intention to tender through the witness and then there is the issue of the witness to come, Mr. Dourel. Can I deal with Mr. Dourel first. Your Honour will have seen the Prosecution's proposed amended witness list which gives rise to a number of issues which will call upon a response from the Defence. One of them and the only one that is pressing in the sense that it presses against the Prosecution's intention to put Mr. Dourel in the witness box tomorrow is that as the Trial Chamber will, I think, appreciate, Mr. Dourel's report is, in effect, a comment on certain of the conclusions reached in Professor Lecomte's report. And when the Prosecution indicated its intention to as Mr. Dourel to the Prosecution's witness list, certainly so far as we were concerned our consent at that stage was certainly premised on the assumption that the Prosecution intended to call Professor Lecomte to give evidence before the Trial Chamber, she having been on the Prosecution's witness list since the outset. And Your Honour will recall that during the course of the evidence of Professor Aleksandric, the Prosecution through Mr. Re indicated that it would indeed tender Professor Lecomte's report and Professor Aleksandric was dispatched with a request to provide a critique of it. Mr. Dourel's is also a critical aspect of Professor Lecomte's report. So when the Prosecution's proposed amended witness list was filed on Friday it came as some surprise to me to discover that the Prosecution intended to abandon Professor Lecomte and not to call her to give evidence before the Trial Chamber, particularly since there is to be evidence from two witnesses which is in effect a comment on the evidence that was to be elicited from Professor Lecomte. So there are two difficulties as matters currently stand. Mr. Dourel is on a proposed list, it's obviously rather short notice to be calling forensic evidence of that nature, particularly when we haven't heard from the author of the report upon which he is, in effect, being invited to comment so that she hasn't set out her conclusions and the relevance of insect and larvae to the conclusions that she drew. And so as a matter of logic, there are really two issues that arise. One is the circumstances in which it would be right for the Trial Chamber to have Professor Lecomte's evidence before it and the second is the order in which the evidence is to be called. As I say, we have no objection to the Prosecution adding Mr. Dourel, providing Professor Lecomte is called before the Trial Chamber to explain her conclusions and her reasoning as well. If the Prosecution is adamant that it will not call Professor Lecomte, despite the way in which the matter has proceeded thus far, then I suppose the reluctant position that we would have to adopt would be to invite the Trial Chamber to call Professor Lecomte, but even then it would be certainly more logical for Professor Lecomte to give evidence before those who comment upon her conclusions to give evidence. So the main concern that I have is that in effect the Prosecution has added Mr. Dourel and taken away Professor Lecomte on whose conclusions he is being invited to comment. So that is our immediate concern. There are, as I say, a number of other issues about the way in which the Prosecution re-ordered its witness list which require to be addressed, but they don't need to take up Trial Chamber time at the moment and could be addressed in the course of a short written submission to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I join in Mr. Emmerson's remark but would only like to add that in the filing with regard to the submission of this particular witness's report, that's Mr. Dourel's report on August 16th, the Prosecution states the Prosecution requested this report on the 25th July 2007. It clarifies and provides further details about forensics issues relating to the September 1998 body recovery operation at the Lake Radonjic canal site which were the subject of the two expert reports of forensic expert Professor Dominique Lecomte. So it is very clear that this was a supplemental report to follow in light of that information that had been obtained by the Prosecution with regard to the forensic pathological issues that exist in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Professor Lecomte has provided two reports. The first one was on the 27th of October last year and the second one was on the 15th of June this year. The original purpose of a report from Professor Lecomte was to examine or have an outside expert examine the methodology of the Serbian forensic recovery process in 1998 and to give an independent and learned critique and commentary on how it was carried out. As you're aware, her conclusions are generally that it was carried out as well as it could have been under the circumstances. The Prosecution is satisfied, having heard the evidence of so far Professor Aleksandric and Dunjic that her conclusions are consistent with the evidence that the Trial Chamber has heard and the Trial Chamber could, in our respectful submission, come to that conclusion themselves without Professor Lecomte's -- without burdening the Trial Chamber with additional witnesses and Professor Lecomte. Professor Lecomte provided a second report this year, and it appears to the Prosecution that Professor Lecomte went outside the area of her expertise in providing an opinion which she was probably not as well equipped to make in relation to the presence or otherwise of larva in bodies or in a forensic site as someone who has that particular area of expertise as a specialty. When Professor Aleksandric testified in July, the Trial Chamber, in fact, the Presiding Judge, Judge Orie, asked questions of Professor Aleksandric directed towards to the presence or otherwise of larva or maggots in the bodies of what he was observed when he was carrying out -- when -- at the time. To cover a gap between what we saw as a deficiency in Professor Lecomte's second report and the questions the Trial Chamber was asking, on the 25th of July or in that week we asked -- we sought an expert, a suitably qualified entomologist and it's a highly specialised field, forensic entomology, and we found all sort -- the opinion of Mr. Dourel, Laurent Dourel, Lieutenant Laurent Dourel of the national gendarmerie of France, and you can see from the curriculum vitae which is filed with his report that he has 700 expertise since 1992, of which about 70 to 80 have been have been in relation to forensic entomology solely. He is a world expert in the area of forensic entomology, and particularly in Europe. If anyone is qualified to give the opinion the Trial Chamber it appeared to us was seeking to find more information on, that is presence or otherwise of larva or maggots when bodies are recovered in situ, it is Mr. Dourel or someone of his expertise. I just correct myself. A moment ago I said he has 700 expertise, it's actually the institute for which he works in Paris, not him -- not Mr. Dourel himself. And on that basis we obtained the report and we put him on the witness list. Why are we calling him tomorrow? Well, the Trial Chamber is aware of that, as are the Defence, in that we had a difficulty obtaining other witnesses next week because the witnesses we had planned to call became unavailable. And Mr. Dourel is in Paris and he was the easiest and most convenient witness to call in the time available. We filed the motion on the 17th of August this year, and we -- and the Defence has had his report since the first week of August, the week after we obtained the report, had it translated into English. So the Defence in our submission should be well prepared to cross-examine Mr. Dourel on this issue because they in fact should have been prepared to cross-examine Professor Aleksandric, Professor Dunjic when they testified in July so in our submission there can be no prejudice to the late notice. Of course, if there is any issue we would of course listen to any submissions that Defence counsel would make about the need they would have to -- for additional time to prepare their cross-examination. But at the moment it doesn't appear to us in our submission that they would need it. So those are the reasons why we seek to add him to the list. It provides -- the evidence he provides is not merely a commentary on Professor Lecomte's report and in fact it is not intended as a comment on Professor Lecomte's report, it's actually intended to fill a gap in relation to the presence or otherwise of maggots and what it means in relation to how long the bodies might have been there and it's something which in our submission Professor Lecomte is not qualified to comment on in the same way that Mr. Dourel is. So in our submission he is the most appropriate witness to cover that particular area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the 23rd of April of this year, Mr. Dutertre wrote to Professor Lecomte and her colleague, drawing attention to questions that had been raised about the integrity of the crime scene and the possibility that bodies may have been moved post mortem, and basing themselves no doubt on their knowledge of her sphere of expertise, they asked her to address four specific questions with that potential outcome in mind. First of all, an estimation of the date of death for each body based on the available video, photographic, and post mortem findings; secondly, the period for which, that is to say the period of time for which each body had been in situ at the site where it was recovered; thirdly, any other forensic medical conclusions capable of being drawn; and fourthly, "to submit any other comments that may be useful for determination of the authenticity of the three crime scenes where the relevant bodies were discovered." Professor Lecomte then goes through each set of remains one by one, looking at the state of the remains, not simply at the question of dipteral larva, although that is one of the factors that in some instances she chooses to refer to, but also the presence or absence of complete skeletons. What inference is there to be drawn from the location of the skeleton and the missing bones where they are missing, and a variety of other indicia which lead her to express certain conclusions. If I can summarize it very briefly, her conclusions in respect of the remains recovered adjacent to the canal are consistent with the proposition that the remains had been moved sometime shortly before they are recorded as having been found. Just to take a random illustration, she will say, for example, in respect of a particular set of remains that the date of death can be placed at more than three months, not taking account of all of the environmental features, including larvae but not confined to it, it is her opinion that the body has been in situ for a very short period of time. She also draws certain conclusions about the bodies that have been removed from the indictment that were recorded as having been discovered in and around the economic farm.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, could you please come closer to the microphone, you are very hard away from it and the interpreters are having a hard time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I do apologise. The remains that were recovered in and around the economic farm where she has drawn conclusions about dates of death, which are consistent of the dates of reported disappearance and would place those dates of death at a time after the area had been secured by Serbian forces. Now, plainly she is an important witness in evaluating the other evidence that the Trial Chamber has heard, and for Mr. Re in effect to suggest that her conclusions are premised solely upon the presence or absence of dipterous larvae and the development of insects in relation to the bodies is obviously inconsistent with the way in which she expresses herself in her report. As far as cross-examination is concerned, I have to say candidly that because of the way in which her report was presented and the way in which the Prosecution then served the report of Mr. Dourel, it had been our confident expectation that Professor Lecomte would explain her reasons to the Trial Chamber and that therefore Mr. Dourel's gloss or qualifications of what can be inferred from dipterous larvae would be before the Trial Chamber as part of the overall picture of the evidence. So that is the position as we submit it. It would in our submission be quite wrong for the Prosecution now to be permitted to substitute, effectively, a witness who supports their case for one who arguably does not -- or indeed to suggest to the Trial Chamber that the conclusions that Professor Lecomte expressed in direct answer to questions that the Prosecution expressly put to her and must, therefore, have concluded were within her expertise should now be discarded on the basis that somehow overall her conclusions lie outwith her expertise. So, Your Honour, those are our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I just briefly respond. Only one thing in relation to whether or not we would call Professor Lecomte. In a sense, we're in the Trial Chamber's hands. I mean, the Trial Chamber is clearly making the assessment at the end of the case. If it's of assistance to the Trial Chamber, if you're of that view, we will call Professor Lecomte, if you feel that it's necessary to get a complete picture as to how the forensic process was carried out by the Serbs at the -- Serbian authorities at the time. However, we would not rely upon that portion of her second report in which she bases an opinion in relation to the presence or otherwise of larvae because now despite what Mr. Emmerson's just said, she has in our submission gone outside her area of expertise and she wouldn't be the first expert before this Tribunal or any other to have done so, in an attempt to be helpful. So if it's of assistance we would make application to put her back on the list. We make it clear, we don't rely upon that. Mr. Dourel we would say is the preferred expert in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You've said several times Professor Lecomte is not the first expert in this field and she went beyond her expertise. That's -- the first sentence suggests that there are better ones and the second sentence suggests that she should have stayed out it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I meant was clearly in the experience of everyone in this courtroom experts sometimes go outside their area of expertise. I just mean that in general. What I meant in the second -- in relation to the second area, having read her opinion we are of the view in relation to the larvae and the presence of maggots, et cetera she is wrong and Mr. Dourel the expert in that particular field of forensic entomology is correct and we do not wish to put her second report or that portion of it in which she expresses an opinion which we say, A, goes outside her expertise and, B, is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the matter during the first break. We don't find it useful to do it at this very moment, but we'll give it full priority today.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could I just invite the Trial Chamber whilst doing that, for example, to have a look at her conclusions and the reasons for them, in respect just to take as an example of body R-3 where she concludes the body has been dead for three months and one of the bases for her conclusion that the body has only been in situ for a short time is that there has been no colonization of the remains, not by dipterous larvae but by grass or branches that one would expect to have grown into it if it had been there since it had died. That's the sort of general conclusion that she reaches quite independent of the issue of larvae development.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say it's not just the little animals, but there's more.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly. Can I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's -- well, hold on for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There also remains another issue which is what is the propriety of the Prosecution moving at this time based upon the information they have received from Professor Lecomte and withdrawing her from the witness list. There's also another legal issue with regard to the prosecutoral duty and obligations to in the broadest sense seek justice and to assist the Trial Chamber independent of the specific issues as they relate to factual matters that have been presented through her report, and we would, if the Court deems it appropriate, wish to give submissions on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, there's another question I would have, that is: Is this now -- but perhaps my memory doesn't serve me well enough. Is this the first time that you take the position that the report of Professor Lecomte on this specific aspect is going beyond her expertise or have you expressed this view also at a time when we just had received this report and where others were invited to comment on it. Was it -- at that time did you already say there was no need to comment on that because that part of the report is -- was beyond her expertise anyhow, so we'll not rely on that, we'll just ignore that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is my question clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If your question is directed to when did the Prosecution form the view that Professor Lecomte --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you expressed that view for the first time, is that today or was it done earlier? Perhaps, if you hadn't developed it, then you couldn't express it, that's clear. But I just wanted to know if my memory serves me well if my recollection is that I'm now -- it's now for the first time put that Professor Lecomte here went well beyond her expertise as far as this aspect of her report is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It probably is the first time we've expressed it in court, but clearly the fact that we sought Mr. Dourel's expertise in July meant that we were thinking about it and especially when the Trial Chamber asked questions to Professor Aleksandric and it became an issue. From when we got it we were concerned about what it said, but whether we expressed it in court before, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course for the Chamber to give specific attention to whether the concerns are about the conclusions or about the methods and the expertise of the witnesses -- yes. Anything else at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Not on that matter. May I turn to the question of exhibits with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Briefly. This morning Mr. Re notified the Defence and the Trial Chamber of a number of exhibits that he proposes to seek to use with the next witness. I don't think there's any question about protective measures in respect of the next witness. I'm pausing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is not aware of any -- next witness, no protective measures applied for nor to be expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are no protective measures sought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So far as Mr. Repic is concerned, the -- I don't know whether Your Honours have seen the e-mail that was sent by the Prosecution, but in effect the suggestion is that through this witness the Prosecution seeks to use four statements taken from arrested, detained suspects between June of 1998 and March of 1999 concerning the disappearance of Rade Popadic and his colleague. Your Honours will recall Rade Popadic's remains, partial remains, were recovered from the canyon section in September. These statements, Your Honours, are statements that were not taken by this witness whose testimony from his statement makes it clear that he himself has no knowledge, direct or indirect, of the circumstances of their death beyond the fact that having been dispatched from Baballoq to Junik, the two individuals did not arrive at their destination. And we respectfully object to the admission through this witness of statements taken allegedly from suspects under interrogation, who from the content of their statements do not appear to have any direct knowledge and cite no source for allegations that are made that these individuals were arrested and detained and captured and then killed as opposed, for example, to dying in some other way perhaps in the context of an exchange of fire. So they are four statements taken by the security service, and we respectfully object to their introduction through this witness. And indeed given that they are individuals who could properly testify, the Prosecution has given no intention of any intention to take statements from them or to call them. They can be in our submission of no probative value to the Trial Chamber in those circumstances. They're not in the same category as the statements that were examined in relation, for example, to Zenel Alija and Bekim Kalamashi where it was by common agreement that those statements were not put forward as evidence of the truth of their contents but as evidence of the progress of the investigation that was taking place and its integrity. But these, as we say, late statements are in our submission entirely outside that category. This witness is not in a position to speak to them. I think Mr. Re can confirm he's never seen them before. I don't know whether he's been shown them since he arrived in The Hague, but they are entirely outside any evidence that he is in a position to give and we would respectfully submit that they should not be admitted or indeed used in evidence with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, would you please respond to that. Also a distinction has been made by Mr. Emmerson between the Kalamashi statements et cetera which he said served some other purpose. Just from the e-mail I cannot see what purpose, what probative value you find in the four statements, the fact that they were given or the truth of their content. I'm not aware of that. Please respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I express some surprise that Mr. Emmerson has decided to use court time to debate this particular issue when I informed him earlier when he rang me that I did not intend to tender those two statements through the witness but merely have them marked for identification. And when a witness from the DB testifies within the next few months -- sorry, next few weeks, to have that person identify where the statements have come from. The only reason why I would show them to this witness and have them identified as Serbian government statements is to set the process in chain. I'm not intending to tender them through this particular witness. I will make the appropriate submissions at the appropriate time about their relevant and probative weight, given that they are corroborating each other and the events with which this witness will testify about. So my intention is not to tender them, but to show them to the witness, have the witness identify them as Serbian government statements, taken by DB or MUP and leave it at that for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it would be more appropriate for these statements to be tendered at a time when he has an appropriate witness to deal with that information as opposed to doing it in this fashion. At this time -- and I echo the remarks made by Mr. Emmerson. And it's really cluttering up the record. There's no reason for this to occur at this time. There is no indicia of reliability whatsoever. We have no information at all concerning the circumstances under which these statements were taken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I do understand from Mr. Re the main purpose of having them marked for identification and to ask the witness about is to say are these the kind of statements that were recorded at the time and not tendering them, so to that extent if you say would it be more appropriate for these statements to be tendered at a time he has an appropriate witness to deal with that information, as far as the content is concerned, I think that Mr. Re takes the same position. As far as -- I mean, if we would have to recall Mr. Repic at that time to say, Well, this is a kind of document --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- produce them at the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which he won't. The witness who he seeks to tender the statements through theoretically should be in a position to say these are the kind of statements that are taken by the Serbian police at certain times based on the information that I have from Mr. Re is that he plans on doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course the Chamber doesn't know exactly through which witnesses these statements will then later be tendered. Let me just consult my colleagues -- or is there any other -- Mr. Harvey, you have been --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I join entirely in everything that's been said, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber within the limits just set out by Mr. Re, that is, he's not going to tender these documents, that, therefore, he's not relying on the truth of the statements which are therein but mainly focusing on the format of the statement as such, the Chamber will not disallow Mr. Re to do that. But as may be clear, of course the Chamber is not aware yet of the circumstances under which Mr. Re thinks that he could tender them as far as to their content. And of course the Chamber will then consider whether it's appropriate to do that. And if they then are tendered and if we would decide that they would be admitted, then of course we have a statement of the present witness on -- on the format. Of course the Chamber is not aware whether it will be a person who made a lot of these statements who will be the witness later on through which to tender or someone who gave the statement who might not be fully familiar with the usual way of putting statements on paper. So therefore, within the limited -- within the limited purpose set out by Mr. Re, the Chamber will not disallow him to have these documents marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With that in mind, when Mr. Re chooses to have those documents marked for identification, just so that we don't have a slippage in terms of issues that come up in the future, could he please identify specifically for the record that these are the documents we have been discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, if you at a certain moment tender them say you remember these are the documents already -- he will have to do that because he will have to refer to the MFI number, which eventually might become an exhibit number. So therefore, I think the procedures in place already make it reasonable to expect --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine, I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that attention will be drawn to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: For the record, they're in Rule 65 ter Exhibit 1973 [sic], four documents within that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's not exactly what -- but let's -- there seems to be no problem in this respect. Mr. Re, are you ready to call your next witness and who's going to examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Rade Repic, I call him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Repic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Usher will now hand out this solemn declaration, the text of it. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Repic. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by Mr. Re, counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Your name is Rade Repic?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your date of birth is the 2nd of December, 1965?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you are currently an officer in the Serbian gendarmerie?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What rank do you hold?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you're based in Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: No. I live in a town in western Serbia and I work in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's what I meant, but I'll take you through -- I'll just take you through some brief details. You went to JNA military academy in 1986?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: From 1990 to 1992 you worked in the MUP in Belgrade as an assistant commander of a police station?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And from 1992 to 1995 in Mali Zvornik, assistant commander of a police station there?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: I started off as deputy commander and I very soon became a commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And from 1995 to 2001, were you the commander of the police station at Sabac in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: The Loznica section within the secretariat of Sabac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you join the PJP, or the special police forces, of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was its role within the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: The role of the special police units, the PJP, in the period between 1992 and the end of 1999 was to maintain law and order, which had been disrupted in areas such as Belgrade and so on and so forth and to assist certain units such as the units in Kosovo where security situations were impaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did the duties of the PJP differ from those of the regular police?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: The difference lay in the fact that the equipment which the PJP units had was of a higher level, the training they underwent was stricter and more complex, and the unit -- the tasks performed by the PJP units were of a more complex nature and involved emergency situations, incidents, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the difference in weaponry the PJP had compared with those of the regular police?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: In Serbia all the members of the MUP had short-barrelled and long-barrelled weapons. The PJP units, in addition to these weapons, whenever the units were used as formations they were also wielding machine-guns and anti-aircraft machine-guns, which meant that they did have more sophisticated weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about vehicles?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: The vehicles, too, differed of course. The regular police forces used passenger vehicles, whereas the members of PJP units used all-terrain vehicles as well, such as Mitsubishi, Nissan makes, TAM-100s, I don't know how to explain this, but these were trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about armoured personnel carriers, did the PJP have those?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: They had APCs, but also these were combat armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Tanks?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Kalashnikovs?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: RPGs?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Rocket-propelled grenades.

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I -- you mean hand-held rocket-launchers?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you have them in the PJP?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how did the uniforms of the PJP differ from those of the regular police?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: The regular units of the Ministry of the Interior, i.e., policemen, wore quite a different uniform which was blue in colour with short-sleeved shirts and peaked caps, whereas members of the PJP units wore camouflage uniforms with greyish colours. They wore caps and protective equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So they were distinctively different?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The reporting chains, how did they differ from those of the regular police, that is, the subordination upwards?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: The chain of command within the PJPs started off with the squad leader, who had up to ten men under him; the next in line was the platoon commander who had 25 men; the next level is that of a company commander who had about 130 to 150 men under his command; and then the commander of a battalion or a detachment who had three to four companies under him depending on the formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm after is how they reported upwards as compared to the regular police? Was there a separate reporting chain of command?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a separate chain of command. From the lowest level the reporting went up to the highest level. The squad commander reported to the platoon commander, the platoon commander in turn reported to the company commander, who reported to his detachment commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm after is: Who did they report to after that, the minister of the interior or someone else?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: The detachment commanders reported to the gendarmerie commander or to the person authorised by him, the person who had been authorised by the gendarmerie commander to be in charge of a given action.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did General Obrad Stevanovic fit in here, what was his job?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: General Obrad Stevanovic was assistant to the minister at the time and was in charge of PJPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that a separate reporting line to that of the normal police? That's all I want you to tell us.

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In 1998, were you a company commander in the PJP, that is, you just described having about 130 to 150 men under their command?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did your duties as a company commander involve, just very briefly?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Duties of a company commander are to take care that his unit is at full strength, to conduct training of his unit, to prepare his unit for activities out in the field, to be in command of the unit in the course of security-related activities and tasks, to deal with any problems that may arise, and to report on any important events or problems to his immediate superior I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And in 1998 who was your immediate superior when you were a company commander?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior was Colonel Branko Prljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And where was he based?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: I don't understand fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did he work from? Where was he physically located?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to answer that question. In 1998 we had various assignments and actions, and this dictated where he was based. We can say that he spent most of the time in the northern part of Kosovo, that's to say in Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you deployed to Kosovo in 1998, just yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Between four and five perhaps, I can't tell you exactly, but not less than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you first go there in 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you the exact date, but I believe it was in March of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you say March?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: March, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did you go to Kosovo the first time?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: We were sent to Kosovo for the first time in order to assist the local security forces because the security situation in Srbica was quite disrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you go in March 1998? Where were you deployed to?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: In the month of March of 1998 we were deployed to the hunting ammunition factory and the local police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long were you there for?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name of the location.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every time I was engaged in Kosovo, I was engaged for the duration of four to six weeks. I wouldn't be able to tell you for that particular occasion. I could tell you that I was there for about a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you go to Junik?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: We went to Junik in the second half of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say "we," did you take a unit with you from Sabac?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Of course. When I say "we went," I meant my unit and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many were in this unit?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact number, but the entire company went there. I suppose that there were around 130 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you get there, by bus?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: We travelled to Kosovska Mitrovica by bus and then via Istok and Pec to Decani, Junik, and Babaloc. We travelled in a convoy with escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you mean by an escort?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: By an escort I meant the security assistance provided by PJP members who were supposed to be relieved by that particular reinforcement and who were in APCs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long did your unit remain in Kosovo in the Junik area in May?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: The entire month of May and part of June, perhaps until mid-June.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why was your unit sent to Junik?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Just as was the case with the month of March, we went to Junik to assist local police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did they require assistance?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: In that period, the intelligence obtained and the local situation indicated that the members of Albanian ethnicity started organizing armed units by arming their members, and they started attacking settlements that were predominantly Serb as well as Albanian settlements that had sided with the Serbs, loyal to Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And which group was doing this?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Do you mean which group exerted pressure?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Our intelligence at the time indicated that these were Albanians from the local settlements near Decani around Junik and around Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did your intelligence tell you anything about the existence of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: In this period they were working intensely on building up the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I would like to have one clarification. Witness, you said in that period the intelligence obtained and the local situation indicated that the members and they started attacking settlements, members of what exactly were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to persons who gave their allegiance to the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But members, because the previous question was about assistance to local police units. So when you were referring to members you were not referring to members of the police units but members of another type of organization?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Perhaps I wasn't clear enough. I meant the local authorities, our colleagues who worked in local police stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you said that those members of those who were working in the police stations, they started attacking and reorganizing -- they started attacking settlements which were predominantly Serb but also Albanian settlements that had sided with the Serbs. Is that -- so police persons organizing themselves to attack local settlements or -- I'm still struggling with the word "member" you used or was it your intention to say that by organizing themselves and attacking settlements they became members of those units or that finally performed these attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will clarify this. We were sent there to help the local authorities, i.e., the local police units because ethnic Albanians, members of the Albanian people started arming themselves up. As a result of this, vehicles travelling along roads came under frequent attacks, as did settlements predominantly inhabited by Serbs. And there was pressure put to bear on Albanians who were loyal to Serbs, to Serb representatives of the local authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A little earlier you said that when you arrived you came in buses with armed escort. You said you were in a convoy with armed escort. Why did you require armed escort?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Escort was necessary because from Sipolj, which is a place on the outskirts of Kosovska Mitrovica, all the way through to Decani and Djakovica, along that route there were frequent attacks on vehicles driven by civilians and particularly targeted were police vehicles travelling individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your information about who was doing the attacking?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: The information I spoke a moment -- spoke of a moment ago which indicated that local Albanians were getting organized, those who were loyal to the KLA more and more, and that as they were getting armed their attacks increased and their armed formations grew.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What weaponry did you take with you to Kosovo in May 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: The regular weapons I already mentioned that PJP members normally held which were short-barrelled weapons, pistol; long-barrelled weapons, rifle; machine-guns; and hand-held rocket-launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there refugees in the Junik area?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the Junik and Babaloc areas there was -- there were refugee settlements holding the population that fled from the areas of Albania, Croatia, Bosnia, and other war-struck areas at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, let's go to Junik. Where were the refugees in Junik?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: As you set off from Decani in the direction of Junik, about a kilometre ahead of the village of Junik there is a refugee settlement holding, or rather, which held or had about a hundred houses complete with infrastructure and ready to receive and accommodate refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were those refugees from? What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: As I said, the refugees came from Albania among other places. I do recall that there were two or three families from the village of Vrane. This remained etched in my memory. There were also refugees from Bosnia and Croatia there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were they Serbian refugees from Bosnia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: I suppose that they were Serbs -- or at least most of them were. I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly now. Perhaps there were people of other ethnicities too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Had the accommodation been built specifically to house the refugees or was it already there when they arrived?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: I don't know what had existed in the area before the refugee settlement was built. What I do know for a fact is that the settlement was brand new, it had been recently built, it had the necessary infrastructure, the roads, the community building, health centre, police station, all the necessary infrastructure you need to have for a settlement to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let's go to the refugees in Babaloc. Can you describe the refugee situation there?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Two-thirds of the unit under my command was based in Babaloc. The situation was identical as in Junik. The refugees from these regions also had their accommodation there. The refugee settlement was identical to the one in Junik in terms of its structure, size, resources, and so on, except that it was located 4 to 5 kilometres or perhaps even 6 to 7 kilometres from it. It was on the left side of the road travelling from Decani to Djakovica. What was more characteristic is that it was further in the territory under the control of the KLA during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the refugees then accommodated in Babaloc?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that precisely, but I know for a fact that they came from different regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were they Serbian, to your knowledge, or Serb?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just said two-thirds of your unit was based in Babaloc. Was the other third based in Junik?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were the members of your unit staying in the same accommodation as the refugees?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: That's correct. In both refugee settlements we used houses on the outskirts for accommodating our unit, the houses that did not have refugees living in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you in Junik or Babaloc?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: I was in Junik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the security situation in relation to the refugees in Junik and in Babaloc, firstly dealing with Junik?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Upon my arrival in Junik, my arrival and that of my unit, we realised that the situation was a bit more favourable in Junik and this is why we opted to base there only one-third of the deployed unit. The village of Junik was known as one of the largest villages in the former Yugoslavia. The estimates were that the village had between 7 and 9.000 inhabitants at the time. During that period of time in cooperation with the commander of the local police we went frequently into the village for patrol duty. We communicated with local residents, and we visited the Serb houses which were on the outskirts of Junik, a couple of them were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there any attacks on refugees in Junik during the month you were there from May to June 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, there were no instances of provocation by Junik residents against the refugees, in the refugee settlement. The refugees mostly encountered problems when they went to Decani for their own personal needs. On their way there, they would be met and mistreated or their IDs checked by illegal organs, that is to say, uniformed individuals representing the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you come to know about this?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Fortunately, the majority of people who had encountered problems returned back to the refugee settlement and this is how we learned about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said the majority returned back. Are you suggesting that some didn't return?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be able to say precisely. There were cases where it was reported that a certain refugee had not returned; however, it remained unresolved whether they had been taken away by the KLA or whether their departure from the refugee settlement was of their own accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that some refugees would be met and mistreated or their IDs checked by people representing the KLA. What do you know about them being mistreated?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Well, the mere fact that an armed group of people stopped you on the road, that they took you out of your car, searched you, confiscated your documents, IDs, and so on, made your situation unsafe and it was certainly unpleasant for people experiencing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let's go to Babaloc. You talked about Junik. Let's go to the refugees and the security situation of the refugees in Babaloc in May/June 1998. How did it differ from Junik?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: The difference between the refugee settlement in Babaloc and that one in Junik was that the one in Babaloc was closer to the villages where the KLA was in majority and where it was almost impossible for local authorities to operate in safe conditions. One couldn't send a single patrol of local policemen to carry out any task in the villages that were in the hinterland of Babaloc. In addition to that, there were daily provocations against the village of Babaloc, the refugees in the Babaloc refugee settlement, and the units securing them. Those were armed provocations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just please describe to the Trial Chamber what you mean by armed provocations; what happened?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: When I say "provocations," I'm referring to a situation where you had daily problems with your security organs who were in observation posts, where they were supposed to take -- to ensure safety of the citizens, and they came under fire, they were fired at. So we needed trenches, we needed to ensure safety for those people so that they could carry out their duties properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were these observation posts?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: In the outskirts of the settlement, near the Rastavica intersection, near the villages around Radonjic Lake and at the elevation which is above Babaloc, I'm now having difficulty remembering the exact toponym, but it was some sort of an elevation, feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you referring to Erecka Suka?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You referred a moment ago to -- you said one couldn't send a single patrol of local police to carry out any task in the villages that were in the hinterland of Babaloc. Which area are you referring to when you say the hinterland of Babaloc?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Towards Radonjic Lake, towards the following villages: Rznic, Dubrava, and another five or six villages there, towards the lake, on the left side of the road travelling from Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was the MUP or PJP able to go into that area at that time, that is, the villages you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Well, unless there was a dire necessity, even PJP would not enter those villages because it had already been clear what was under the control of the KLA. And protection was provided only in order to unblock the roads and in order to ensure normal daily activities for people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just clarify what you mean by the last line, "protection was provided only in order to unblock the roads," which roads are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the main roads between the following centres: Djakovica, Decani, Pec, and when I say that we did not enter villages unless there was a dire necessity, I mean to say that we did our best to avoid provoking any clashes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You mean with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you were there in Junik and Babaloc in May to June 1998, did you or your unit go into those villages, that is, to the left of the road from Decan?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: We were not given such tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there any attacks on refugees in or from Babaloc in May/June 1998 when you were there?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your information about how many KLA were in the area on the left of the Decan road?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Our official intelligence indicated that during that period of time in that sector around a dozen or so villages in that area, there were already 600 armed and trained members of the KLA. There was information indicating that there was a far greater number of armed men who only possessed weapons but did not have full equipment, uniform and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there any KLA check-points to your knowledge on local roads or main roads in that period in that area?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: There were local check-points and there were armed guards in front of every village on the local roads. I would use a military term for them, in fact, and I would call them ambushes and not guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you know they were there?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Every attempt on the part of local authorities was thwarted either by stopping them, checking them, or opening fire against policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I'm looking at the clock. Would this be a suitable time to have a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break until a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we -- I give you an opportunity, Mr. Re, to continue the examination-in-chief of the witness, the Chamber has considered the -- has considered the issue raised in view of experts to be called. First of all, Mr. Repic, I have to deal with a matter which doesn't affect you in any way at this moment, so I apologise for raising a matter. Just Ignore what I'm saying. I'm addressing the parties at this moment. Mr. Re, the Chamber is inclined to believe that it would assist the Chamber to hear all the expert evidence related to the matters we discussed before the break. That would mean that it is suggested that you would call the expert Lecomte and not only the expert Dourel. At the same time, the Chamber is a bit concerned about having witnesses here, sending them back home, recalling them in order to respond to all the criticisms. I think that a well-accepted - but please correct me when I'm wrong - a well-accepted difference between witnesses and experts is that usually experts, unlike witnesses, are allowed to attend the testimony of other experts so that they have first-hand knowledge of what the other expert said. I also do understand that you have some difficulties in getting other witnesses for later today. So the Chamber has asked itself whether it would still be possible to explore the possibility of having witnesses Lecomte and Dourel in court, both of them by let's say Wednesday and Thursday. I do understand that it doesn't entirely fit into your plans, but at the same time -- of course the Chamber is less concerned about who comes first and who responds at what moment to whatever criticism the one has expressed in view of the opinions of the other. So there is still an opportunity that the expert could even follow the proceedings if it would be impossible to have two experts together in court. It would still be a possibility to -- even the internet would or a videotape or video -- DVD would make that possible, because it doesn't make much sense to put all kind of questions to experts, referring to what the other expert said with the -- the expert himself is far better equipped to understand what the other expert had said. Mr. Re, at this moment the Chamber has not made any decisions, but I think we understood at least from what you said that you were willing to seriously consider what the Chamber -- what the Chamber thought would assist it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If the Chamber wants Professor Lecomte, we will call Professor Lecomte. In terms of the scheduling, I understand that Mr. Dourel is available on Tuesday and Wednesday this week only and then not again until October. I have no idea about Professor Lecomte and I don't know about her ability to read an English transcript and I very much doubt there would be a French transcript available by Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have no transcripts available, but I always have to ask the technicians to what extent the French channel with the video would already be available and I do not know whether the French translation can be followed on the internet. I think it could. I'm not quite sure, but certainly something to explore because then we could even consider to invite -- of course to the extent possible, I don't know whether Professor Lecomte has -- might have a very busy schedule, but if she could follow part of the testimony given by the expert Dourel and then join Wednesday, that even might be a solution. But the Chamber would suggest that you actively explore possibilities to have the evidence of both these experts before the Chamber, and preferably in such a way that we don't have to do things five, six times. That would be our suggestion. If there's any comment on it which the Chamber would have to consider, then of course the Prosecution -- the Defence is in a position to raise that now, although we don't want to have a full debate again on the matter, but just if this is totally unworkable or fundamentally opposed by the Defence, then of course we would like to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Not at all, subject to practicalities, it's a course that in our submission commends itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Re, having dealt with this matter you're invited to continue the examination with the witness. Mr. Repic, we now turn to you again. Again apologies for dealing with other matters which were of some urgency. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Repic, before the break -- just excuse me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if one of the parties could assist me, I tried to find a photograph Babaloc hill on which the settlement appears, but I can't find the number at this moment. If anyone could help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I am in a position to deal with that during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but could you give me the number already so that I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I can. It's D111 and D112.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before the break we were -- I was asking you about the KLA check-points and you were telling the Trial Chamber that you would call them ambushes and not guards on the village entrances and exits. In the period you were there, May/June 1998, was there any difference in the KLA activities at night to those in day; and if so, can you tell the Trial Chamber what was happening at night?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Our information, what we were able to observe and register from our positions, positions from which we secured these two settlements, indicated that there was a certain activity of Albanians in the hinterland of the Junik village; that is to say in the area between Junik and the state border with Albania. All of that was taking place during night-time, late evening and early morning hours, where on a nightly basis we registered movements of a large number of motorised vehicles, tractors. There was certain activity which was not typical for a village which doesn't have illumination and all of that. All of this activity indicated that there were certain preparations going on. People were coming and going from the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: We supposed that during that period of time the activities that we could directly observe meant that they were using local roads to go to the state border and then bring in weapons and ammunition, that is to say military equipment, from the state border back.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, moving --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To the extent that that answer is speculative I think causes problems. He can say what he observed and I have no difficulty with what the gentleman observed. With regard to what was the purpose of any movement, there's no information whatsoever at this point that develops that point other than the speculation on this witness's part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time the question was clear what they were doing, and the witness spontaneously gave the answer as he gave it. So therefore Mr. Re can proceed, and it's rather a comment to the testimony than anything else at this moment, Mr. Guy-Smith. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Moving to another area now, and that is Rade Popadic and Nikola Jovanovic. Who was Rade Popadic?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Rade Popadic was a member of the Ministry of the Interior and he worked as the head of sector in the Secretariat of the Interior in Sabac. That was his regular job as policeman, and then within the PJP unit he was a platoon commander from the Secretariat of the Interior in Sabac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I just interpose for one moment and ask through the Trial Chamber whether the Defence have given us the notification of the exhibits they intend to use in cross-examination. We're just trying to locate them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has this notification been given?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, to the extent that we are going to rely on any exhibits is those that have already been forwarded to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We can't find them. We kindly ask if they would send them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is whether it was sent by e-mail or any other way?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just can't find them in our trial support account. I just ask if they could resend it because we can't locate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could send another copy, that would be appreciated. Mr. Re, where I earlier said to Mr. Guy-Smith that it was comment on the testimony rather than anything else, of course would not mean that an answer which starts by saying: "We supposed that during that period of time the activities that we could directly observe ..." There is some intrinsic problem is what is just a supposition and what is an observation, which is of course not clear in the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll develop that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you recall, Mr. Repic, a few moments ago, you told the Trial Chamber that based on your observations you supposed that they were going to the state border and bringing in weapons and ammunition, that is, military equipment from the state border of Albania, what did you see or hear that led you to conclude that they were bringing in the weapons in from Albania?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Given that this was during night-time, it was difficult to see anything. But what one could hear and conclude based on observation and registering all movements was that there was an activity of motorised vehicles from the village of Junik using local roads in the direction of the border. I can also add that there was a situation where there was no electricity in an entire region and then quite -- quite unusually you see a hamlet that is all illuminated because they have generators producing power, then in the military sense it means that it is a good orientation point for whoever is moving from the border without using any lights.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What time of the night are you talking about, the sudden illumination occurring?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, he didn't say "sudden."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Whatever type of illumination, sudden or otherwise, what time of night are you talking about it occurring?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: This occurred in the late evening hours starting from 11.00 p.m. through to 5.00 a.m., but at any rate it was night hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What led you to believe that weapons were coming from Albania, that is, the traffic was coming from Albania as opposed to going the other way?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: I will go back to the official information that we received from both military and civilian bodies collecting intelligence, which indicated that in the period before 1998 there was the toppling of the regime in Albania, and the weapons of the sort we're discussing could be purchased at low price. All the supply channels of the then-KLA originated in Albania, since the possibilities of purchasing weapons there were on the increase.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just what I'm trying to get at is: What was it about the illumination of the village between 11.00 and 5.00 which led you to believe it was being used to guide people bringing weapons from Albania?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: If you look at it topographically, the state border with Albania is at a given level above the sea. The border area goes down into a valley where the villages of Junik, Babaloc, and others are situated, as well as the road from Pec to Djakovica. If you need to complete any sort of activity without the assistance of the state border and the area around the border, you only need one landmark which is well illuminated. If you end up in a valley, the moment you go uphill again you will be able to observe the landmark that will serve as an orientation point for your journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many times did you see this in May/June 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: I can't give you the precise number. Several times in that period of time. Since we worked in shifts, I suppose that others who were present there observed the same sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what was the PJP response to seeing this?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Specifically, I can only speak of the PJP members who made up my company. Since we had the specific assignment of securing the refugee settlements of Junik and Babaloc, we responded to what we saw by reporting to the superior commands with a view to taking certain measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you go out at night to see what was happening? Did you send some patrols out to those illuminated villages is what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: I've tried to explain to you that my task was to secure the refugee settlement. Such a type of engagement would run contrary to the task that I had been given.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you aware of any other, apart from your own unit within the PJP, any other unit of the MUP or the PJP responding to villages illuminated at night by perhaps going up and seeing what was going on?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Since the locations were situated on the other side - let me explain this to you in topographic terms - on the other side of these settlements and that other side having been under the KLA control. I don't know whether any of the units attempted to enter those villages and find out what was going on and why. I think that would have been far too risky and would have incurred unwanted consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is there anything else on that that the Trial Chamber is interested in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's only -- the witness in his last answer said "locations were situated on the other side" and that other side having been under the KLA control. That's not entirely clear what you mean by the other side, the other side of something, or could you please further explain that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to explain this once more. The state border with Albania is located at a certain level above the sea. From the state border inwards, the land goes downhill slightly leading to the villages that I spoke of, Babaloc and Junik and others, and this is the road leading from Decani to Djakovica. On the other side of that particular road, the -- there is higher ground, it's a gentle slope, and it was on that side that the illumination could be observed, that sort that was used as an orientation point, as a reference point. Had it been otherwise, the lights would not have been visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Last question is: You explained all this to us as why you thought they were smuggling -- smuggling, why they were importing weapons. Now, could a similar observation not observed whatever other contraband or even whatever other legal stuff to be imported or I mean, where's the link with the weapons specifically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we're discussing the period of time when the KLA was working intensively on setting up armed formations and was arming at a much greater speed than before, we concluded that this is the sort of merchandise that was involved. Given the period of time, or rather, it could have been other merchandise, generally speaking. But given the period of time and the circumstances in which it was going on, we inferred that weapons were the merchandise that was being smuggled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, I've asked you about Rade Popadic. Who was Nikola Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Nikola Jovanovic was a member of the Ministry of the Interior holding the rank of sergeant, and he worked in the local police station of the municipality of Ljubovija. He was a young person, he wasn't married, he was a good person and a good member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: His rank was corporal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think you just said "good member of the KLA." Was that the correction you made?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were both Rade Popadic and Nikola Jovanovic members of your PJP company?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: The mistake you mentioned is something I haven't heard, but I do repeat. They were good members of the police and they were members of the company I was in command of.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they come with you from Sabac in May 1998 to Junik?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were they accommodated?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: They were accommodated in the refugee settlement of Junik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were -- where was your unit getting its food and daily supplies from when you were based in Junik?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: The logistics support of my unit was received from the Djakovica secretariat and we received our food-supplies from the kitchens of the Djakovica secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did they get from Djakovica to Babaloc and Junik?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: In that period of time, precisely due to frequent attacks on police vehicles travelling individually and without escort, we resorted to all sorts of things, to go at unpredicted times, to use different types of vehicles, to have our PJP members travel in civilian clothes in order to be as inconspicuous as possible and avoid possible provocations en route as far as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How often was your unit being supplied with food from Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: On a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many times per day?

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What happened with Rade Popadic and Nikola Jovanovic? Go back to the last day you saw them.

utterances.speaker: RADE REPIC
utterances.text: The last day I saw them alive we had regular morning activities which meant getting up, touring the units, conducting controls and inspections in the military sense. I had a morning meeting with Rade Popadic in order to exchange information and issue tasks and solve whatever current issues there were. We went to -- which involved also going to the Djakovica secretariat and picking up the food-supplies for the entire unit for the day and returning to Junik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
